doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Jazz at Indiana University in 1957
summary: No saxophone or jazz offerings; the jazz band started around 1958-59 under Buddy Baker; no jamming in East Hall; Hubbard and Montgomery jamming nearby.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Let me ask you if, you went to Indiana University, correct?
And was there jazz — was jazz recognized anywhere like it is now when you went there?

Oh no. They didn’t offer the saxophone and neither did the Manhattan School of Music. Now that was 1957. I think maybe in 1958 or ’59 they finally started the jazz band for I think a half a credit and you met three times a week I think. And Buddy Baker the trombone player was the leader of that. Yeah it took a while to get going and the practice rooms were at a place called East Hall, it was like a rectangle with a couple of rooms in the center but all the practice rooms on the outside, and he had a particular guy named Herb Shive S-H-I-V-E, and he took care of East Hall. And if he heard you playing jazz he’d come in and [shakes finger]. No jamming. “Hey! Break it up in there, no jamming.” And this was 1957, ’58 you know. And at that time people like Freddie Hubbard and Wes Montgomery would occasionally drive down the 40 miles from Indianapolis over to the Trees Center where you could get a hamburger and a chocolate shake every night you know like from probably from eight until ten or something, and they would come down and just jam. And I probably heard them, but I can’t recall it.

There’s something for me that — it was a sort of similar at SUNY Fredonia but this was years later when I was there, that when students are pursuing something that the administration in the school doesn’t do on their own, it’s actually more special.

Students don’t have that now, so I don’t know if there’s any conclusion about that because certainly jazz is part of almost all music school curriculums, but we’ll get there. We’ll come back to that. Did you have an aha moment, sort of an epiphany along the way about what you do? How did this launch, this idea of people can learn to improvise and I can help them?
